cards.title: Zuckerberg's Meta Takes Down No Kings Instagram During Protest Day

depth.text: Meta **suspended** the **No Kings Instagram account** during a protest day

A commenter said the account hit a **rate limit**, triggering an **automated suspension**. Indivisible said it became visible again after **90 minutes**, but the admin still couldn't post for another three hours.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters think a rate limit triggered an automated suspension; others focus on Meta's power to restrict political speech and question its fairness.

comments.text: My bet is that some sort of auto ban logic kicked in, maybe due to abuse of reporting features. It'd if course be worse if a human moderator took it down or affirmed such a decision but not impossible. Meta and other big tech usually over-relies on automated enforcement because it's easier on their wallets than hiring enough moderators to keep up in near-real time. And it's hella easy for a group…
I wonder if these free-speech absolutists will rail about this? Something tells me probably not.
Careless People by Sarah Wynn-Williams was a great read, highly recommend
I'm literally begging people to start using the Fediverse at this point.
Ok, so what is the actual reason it was suspended? Edit: They hit a rate limit and tripped an automated suspension.

cards.title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour

depth.text: bleached corals can **thrive within days** when they touch a **healthy neighbour**

One commenter says this was seen only in fragments from an individual with the same **genetic makeup**, which may make it hard to scale in the wild. Another explains that bleaching means coral expels algae; it doesn’t mean the coral is **dead**.

cards.camps: Two camps: hopeful commenters call this good news for reefs; skeptics say it only works with genetically identical coral, so it may be of little practical use.

comments.text: Coral gets its color from algae called zooxanthellae, which it depends on for photosynthesis. Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algae. Bleached corals are not dead, and remarkably they can not only let the algae in again but can also select a different algae species to cultivate (changing colour in the process)!. This is thought to be a deliberate survival strategy to…

Having been a diver on the Great Barrier Reef numerous times, the scale of bleaching events means that there is often no non-bleached neighbour for vast distances. Healthy propagation rarely occurs before the brown sludge sets in, then its game over.

Of note: This only occurred for fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic makeup(genet: basic meaning is they are a colony). Presumably, it would be difficult to recreate this at scale in the wild. I did not read past the free to read portion of the article that mentions scaling this is possible. I am curious about the methodology of that. I find it strange that the first observance…
Only if they are clones - genetically identical. So not much use in practice, unfortunately.
So does this mean sicking refrigeration islands in key locations will be the way to stop permanent coral bleaching?

cards.title: Pele – Mermaid diagrams as themeable SVG

depth.text: someone made **diagrams** render as **themeable SVGs**, with colors that change without redrawing them
**Pele** turns Mermaid syntax into SVG; **CSS variables** set colors and fonts, and color changes apply **without re-rendering**. It supports every diagram type built into Mermaid 12.1.0.

comments.text: Anytime I try mermaid for anything more complex than a toy diagram I always end up absolutely frustrated by the arcane and topologically poor layout that is produced. Styling seems like a trivial problem by comparison.

> A flowchart subgraph keeps its own direction even when it links to nodes outside the subgraph. This, in and of itself, is sufficient reason for me to switch, even if it were slower than Mermaid.js. I’ve not even made it through the list yet and I’m sold.

Is pele open source? I tried to find the source code of it but I was unable in finding so Edit: found it, https://github.com/obsidianmd/pele Also folks, this is a good reminder to please have a github icon on the top of the page to easily show git/github links if the app is open source, also helps in the fact that I can star your projects and bookmark them more easily :-D
Does the official Mermaid library still require a full or headless browser environment in order to lay out the SVG? If so, Pele is great news for embedding Mermaid rendering in other places.
Just FYI, "pele" is "mouse" in Latvian. :)

cards.title: Gold is now the top U.S. export

depth.text: gold is now the **top U.S. export**, and the writer suspects much is bound for **China**

since October 2025, gold's **export value** has topped other categories almost every month; February 2026 may have set an **all-time record** for tons exported. The writer suspects a high percentage may be headed to **China**, sometimes via Swiss refineries.

cards.camps: Two camps: some suspect foreign governments or China are behind the export surge; others say it mostly reflects recycling and people selling jewelry.

Global demand for gold—lead by China—is surging. That, in turn, made gold “the…

cards.title: Dam removals are bringing fish back across the northeastern United States

depth.text: people are taking down **old dams**, and **river herring** are coming back to northeastern rivers

At the Bellamy River, fish biologist Nathan Furey’s team uses **PIT tags** to track alewives through rapids left after dams came out. In Plymouth, around 25,000 herring once returned annually; now, many runs exceed **200,000**.

cards.camps: Two camps: dam-removal supporters say removing obsolete dams helps fish and avoids costly repairs; critics say dams provide hydropower and water storage, and favor fish ladders instead.

comments.text: A rewilding organization bought some forest land, downstream from a dam, that used to get seasonal flooding before the dam was built and made an agreement with the dam operators to do artificial seasonal flooding via ditches they dug. The flooded forest has the effect of providing fish nurseries so hatchlings have a chance to hide and grow before the water recedes and they have to return to the…

More good news: after years of fighting, Brookfield Renewable agreed to sell four dams on the Kennebec River which will let Atlantic Salmon go back up river to their spawning territory. This just happened in 2025 and could be a bigger breakthrough than the massive alewife restoration that the article mentions. My understanding is that the first few victories on this were very very hard but it…

This sounded familiar and then I realized I had read the same article a few weeks ago. This is some strange syndication I would propose changing the link to this one: https://biographic.com/death-by-a-thousand-dams/ it’s also way better layout and fewer ads.

As the article alludes, the blueprint/precedent for this kind of work was set in the Klamath river basin in western Oregon. The local tribes deserve a tip of the hat for pushing through the lobbying and suits to get this process started. And a hat tip to all of the people who made the projects as successful as they have been in saving fish populations. IIRC, they ran into some surprises with…

Good for the fish but as winters get warmer these dams will be useful to store rain that doesn't stay put in the mountains as winter snow. This might mean more summer droughts. Also a nice clean source of power. I would rather see fish ladders.

cards.title: Source code of the Estonian online voting system

depth.text: someone put the **Estonian voting system's code** online for **public review**
The repository isn't actively developed, but is **kept up to date** with the **code used for elections**; development is supervised by the **State Electoral Office of Estonia**.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say Estonia's e-voting is widely used and has proved robust and secure; skeptics say software alone cannot secure elections and worry about verification and trust.

comments.text: Fully software, even a combo of software and hardware, cannot by itself make elections secure. Think of the Reflections On Trusting Trust problem, the need to verify firmware, etc. You can't ensure that machines _will_ work correctly, but you _can_ verify that they _did_ . To do verify the machines' functioning after the fact you have to do it very soon after closing of the polls, and you have to…

I'm Estonian. E-voting is widely accepted and used here. We've been doing it since 2001, and extensivelly (first parliamentary e-voting) since 2007.
The fact that it's open source is long known (at least in the IT community) and highly appreciated.
There's no inherent doubt about its validity in the local expert and international community.

Living in Estonia, I have a hard time deciding how I feel about this voting system. Currently, with people trusting the government, this system is great. I can just cast my vote online, like I do everything else here, and I can be reasonably sure that my vote is counted thanks to the aforementioned trust in the system. But I really fear the day that trust erodes. On the other hand, though, once…

There are a lot of folks who, whenever this topic comes up, seem to have no knowledge of the systems which already exist and have actually been used in real elections already. For instance, ElectionGuard has been used in several real elections in the US since 2020[1]. [1]: https://electionguard.vote/

Lots of concerns in the discussion yet the fact is that e-voting is used for quite a long time in Estonia, and proved robust and secure. It will scale well. Check the source code. I believe the Swiss also open sourced their e-voting software.

cards.title: I Became a Citizen of Japan

depth.text: someone spent **years** navigating Japan’s **paperwork-heavy process** before becoming a **citizen**

Derek first tried in **2012**, tried again in **2018**, then submitted his application in February 2025. It was approved, but his case worker called **four days after the notice** appeared in the Official Gazette; Derek says the **arcane, arbitrary process** ultimately taught him the importance of following rules and contributing.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see a demanding process as fitting the weight of citizenship; others worry the barriers clash with Japan’s declining population.

comments.text: It is very sobering to consider the demographic cliff that Japan faces combined with the barriers the government puts up to immigration and naturalization. I sincerely wonder what kind of country Japan will be in 50 years.

Japan is one of those countries that doesn’t allow dual citizenship and they require proof of renunciation. Something to think about for those from other “strong” countries who want to go down that route.

Stopped when he said he waited forever to get naturalized, skipping 6 years, and then saying he never got his permanent resident card, so he was just living off renewed visas, and they thought it was strange. It is strange. A lot of the things he said he needed, would have been done in the permanent residence portion of his time in Japan. Just as it is in any country.

"I don’t think citizenship is a light thing. It is not rational to make it friction-free or fast. I was not ready to naturalize in 2012. The system is arcane and arbitrary, and also worked correctly to weed me out of the process. It impressed upon me the importance of following the rules and making a contribution, which honestly impacted how I behaved and thought thereafter. When I was absolutely…
I'm surprised OP's memory can recall this so well

cards.title: NY announces game ownership bill requiring ownership rather than licensing

depth.text: a New York rep wants buyers to **own games** and keep them **playable after shutdown**

Rep. Ritchie Torres introduced the **Power To The Players Act**, directing the FTC to establish regulations on game ownership. Games with online functionality would need an **offline mode** before their servers are shut down; the bill’s details have not been released.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters want buyers to own games and keep them playable; skeptics worry offline requirements could burden developers or lead to worse versions of games.

comments.text: The headline makes it sound like this is specific to NY, but this is a national bill introduced in the House by a NY rep.

Even better would be broad copyright reforms. Fair Use needs to be expanded and clarified. History has shown players are able to keep games alive themselves by emulators, reverse engineering, custom servers, etc. Expand Fair Use to say that these things are protected if needed to keep the game functional.

I hope there's an indie carveout or something for less than like 200k revenue. And maybe a carveout if your licensing gets pulled. I really want copyright to stay the hell out of the way of just letting players reverse engineer old games, but it's an international thing at this point
Consumers always hope that what they gain from a purchase is ownership.
This is amazing. So glad to see stuff like this happening.

cards.title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results

depth.text: someone built a **Commodore 64 simulator** where you can break chips and watch the **board react**

It models the **ASSY 250407 motherboard** pin by pin: lift a chip leg, short it to ground or +5V, remove a chip, or open a resistor, then watch the monitor, keyboard and signals respond. The odd results are **computed from the circuit**, not chosen to match a known fault. It’s for **learning or diagnosis**, not playing games: the simulation runs slower than real time, and a matching symptom is only a clue, not proof.
data: C64 simulation speed on Apple M3 Max
C64 simulation speed on AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 (Gorgon Halo)
C64 simulation speed on Apple M5 Max

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says the slowdown shows why FPGA is still useful; another sees an optimization opportunity.

comments.text: This is really cool, and a fantastic piece of work. It may come in handy when diagnosing / fixing C64 boards. Stretch goals: * Allow the simulation to run diagnostics carts. * On the 250407 board I have had timing edge cases with PLA replacements - the fix is often to fit a small (~100pF) capacitor on the /CASRAM line to slow it down a bit. The cap is fitted from the left leg of an existing 82…

I remember Byuu (RIP) wrote an article around ~10 years ago talking about why BSNES/Higan was "slow", explaining that it's really not slow given what it's trying to do. The more accurately you simulate the chips, there is simply more over overhead involved with synchronization and whatnot. I remember in that article they mentioned a Pong circuit simulation like this that was getting something…
Amazing. Sadly, it can't run in real time even on strong real hardware. I wonder if its code could be optimized to run in real time?

I have been working on this exact same thing. Using real hardware, I am trying to simulate down to the jail bars that are caused by the design. LLMs make this kind of development really approachable. What is fascinating is I can now build components that work through an Arduino to interface with real accessories and C64s.
This is really cool but... At some point, don't we have to start simulating things like internal interference in the conductors, induction, and sending/receiving radio signals?

cards.title: Amazon uses AI to monitor union risk in UK warehouses

depth.text: Amazon's **AI tool** scores warehouse **union risk**, though it says Atlas isn't currently used in the UK

The documents say **Atlas** amasses hundreds of data points—from Reddit posts and staff survey answers to workplace details—to score warehouses from 100 to 900; **lower scores mean greater union risk**. Amazon says it doesn't track individual workers' opinions or union membership, and that Atlas **isn't currently used in the UK**.

comments.text: There is no form of surveillance that does more good than harm in the long run. The endless debates about the value of "catching bad guys" or "keeping people on their best behavior" should be rightly seen as opposed to the fundamental notion that human beings are capable of cooperation and altruism at scale. No amount of mass surveillance is justifiable, and there is no version of the future in…
> I am optimistic about the future of AI at Amazon It's scary to think that any answer but "Strongly Agree" will very likely flag you as a risk. Is this really the society we want?

glossary.rate limit: A rule that caps how often someone can make requests to a site.
glossary.automated suspension: A temporary account block triggered by software rather than a person.
glossary.zooxanthellae: Algae that live in coral and help it get energy.
glossary.photosynthesis: The process algae use to turn sunlight into food.
glossary.genet: A group of corals that share the same genetic makeup.
glossary.Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis: The idea that coral may change the algae it hosts to better suit different conditions.
glossary.horizontal gene transfer: When living things pass genetic instructions between one another outside of having offspring.
glossary.Mermaid: A text-based way to describe a diagram so a tool can draw it.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.CSS variables: Named settings in a webpage's styling that you can reuse, such as a color or font.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.FOUC: Flash of Unstyled Content: the brief moment when a page appears before its intended look has loaded.
glossary.subgraph: A smaller group of connected steps inside a diagram.
glossary.reserve asset: Something a country's government keeps as a store of value it can use when needed.
glossary.U.S. Treasury debt: Money the U.S. government has borrowed and still owes.
glossary.central bank: A country's main public bank, which manages money and keeps reserves.
glossary.refinery: A place that cleans up and reshapes gold so it can be sold or used.
glossary.PIT tag: Passive integrated transponder: a tiny tag that helps researchers recognize a fish when it passes a reader.
glossary.diadromous fish: Fish that spend parts of their lives in fresh water and parts in the ocean.
glossary.fishway: A sloping ramp that lets fish get past a dam.
glossary.NOOMBY: Not Out of My Backyard: a label for people who oppose a project near their home.
glossary.source code: The written instructions that tell a computer how to run a program.
glossary.e-voting: Casting votes electronically, rather than using a paper ballot.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.CVR: Cast Vote Record: an electronic record of votes cast in an election.
glossary.RNG: Random number generator: a tool or program that produces numbers meant to seem unpredictable.
glossary.risk limiting audit: A check that uses a sample of paper ballots to catch an election result that may be wrong.
glossary.naturalization: Becoming a citizen of a country where you were not born.
glossary.permanent residency: Permission to live in a country indefinitely, rather than renewing a temporary visa.
glossary.family register: Japan’s official record of a person’s family relationships and key life events.
glossary.Official Gazette: A government publication where official notices are announced.
glossary.Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT: A test of how well someone can use Japanese.
glossary.FTC: Federal Trade Commission: a US agency that investigates businesses and enforces rules meant to protect consumers.
glossary.revocable license: Permission to use a game that a company can take away, rather than something you own.
glossary.offline mode: A way to play a game without connecting to its servers.
glossary.community servers: Servers that players set up and run themselves so they can keep playing together.
glossary.peer-to-peer: A setup where computers talk directly to each other instead of relying on one central server.
glossary.DRM: Digital Rights Management: restrictions in software that control how it can be copied or used.
glossary.Fair Use: A legal rule that allows some uses of copyrighted work without the owner’s permission.
glossary.first sale doctrine: A rule that generally lets someone resell a copy they legally bought.
glossary.copyright: Legal protection that gives creators control over how their work is copied and shared.
glossary.netlist: A map of which electrical connections on a board are joined together.
glossary.oscilloscope: A display that lets you watch an electrical signal change over time.
glossary.PLA: Programmable Logic Array: a chip that helps direct computer requests to the right part.
glossary.FPGA: Field-programmable gate array: a chip that can be set up for different hardware jobs after it is made.
glossary.union-busting: Actions meant to stop workers from forming or joining a union.
glossary.industrial action: When workers act together, often by striking, to push their employer to change something.
glossary.risk score: A number meant to estimate how likely something is to happen.
